headline: Helicopters rescue 80 people from Grand Canyon flood

sources.title: About 80 people were rescued during Grand Canyon flooding, officials say (AP News)

chunks.text: A [[flash flood]] {{swept through}} Bright Angel Canyon, in Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, on Saturday, August 29, 2026. Up to an inch of rain fell in about 30 minutes. The water {{tore down}} nearly all the [[footbridges]] over Bright Angel Creek near Phantom Ranch, a [[stopover]] for hikers and river [[rafters]]. Rain also fell on the [[burn scar]] of the Dragon Bravo Fire of July 2025, where bare ground {{speeds up}} [[runoff]].

verbs.correct: To move fast across an area
verbs.wrong: To rise slowly for many hours
verbs.why: A cold wind sweeps through the streets in January, and a new fashion can sweep through a whole school in a week. A flash flood swept through Bright Angel Canyon on Saturday, August 29, 2026.

verbs.wrong: To slowly weaken over many years
verbs.why: The city tore down the old stadium to build apartments, and workers tear down a stage the day after a concert. The floodwater tore down nearly all the footbridges over Bright Angel Creek.

verbs.wrong: To absorb water like a sponge
verbs.why: A good coffee speeds up your morning, and a new computer speeds up the whole office. Bare ground on the burn scar of the Dragon Bravo Fire speeds up runoff when it rains.

chunks.text: Rescue teams {{brought in}} helicopters, and searchers used [[night vision]] equipment to find people in the dark, the incident commander said. By sunset on Saturday, 45 people had been rescued, and 37 more were {{flown out}} on Sunday, about 80 in total. The Red Cross {{looked after}} them at a lodge on the South Rim. Rangers then {{went through}} [[permit records]] and checked [[license plates]] to count who was still missing.

verbs.wrong: To return people to their homes
verbs.why: A restaurant brings in extra staff for a busy weekend, and a school brings in a specialist to fix its computers. Rescue teams brought in helicopters to carry people out of the canyon.

verbs.correct: To leave a place by aircraft
verbs.wrong: To pass above an area in a plane
verbs.why: Fans fly out the morning after the final, and a sick tourist may be flown out to a bigger hospital. By Sunday, 37 more people had been flown out of the canyon, about 80 in total.

verbs.wrong: To try to find a missing person
verbs.why: Grandparents often look after the kids during school breaks, and a nurse looks after ten patients on a night shift. The Red Cross looked after the evacuees at a lodge on the South Rim.

verbs.correct: To examine records one by one
verbs.wrong: To count people as they arrive
verbs.why: An accountant goes through every receipt at tax time, and a coach goes through the video of the last game. Rangers went through permit records and checked license plates to count who was missing.

chunks.text: Two people died: a 46-year-old [[chiropractor]] and a 42-year-old man who owned a [[martial arts]] studio, both from Texas. A third friend, a 53-year-old pilot from Wyoming, was still missing on September 3, when more than 100 [[searchers]] with helicopters, [[drones]] and dogs {{kept on}} looking. The three men had {{set out}} for several days of hiking and fishing, and last {{checked in with}} their families on Thursday, August 27.

verbs.why: The band kept on playing after the power failed, and a good student keeps on trying after a bad grade. More than 100 searchers kept on looking for the missing pilot on September 3.
The family set out for the beach before sunrise, and the climbers set out from base camp at midnight. The three men had set out for several days of hiking and fishing in the canyon.
Students check in with their parents after a long flight, and a manager checks in with the team every Monday. The men last checked in with their families on Thursday, August 27.

chunks.text: The flood also {{knocked out}} the park's main water [[pipeline]], 12.5 miles long and the only one it has. About 40 percent of it is damaged, the park's deputy superintendent said, and the South Rim has about two weeks of water [[in storage]]. Hotels stopped taking [[overnight guests]] on August 31, and visitors were asked to {{cut down on}} showers. A $208 million [[upgrade]] of the pipeline, begun in 2023, may now {{fall behind}} schedule. On September 3 the park {{closed off}} more trails, with no [[reopening date]].

verbs.correct: To stop a system from working
verbs.wrong: To fill a channel with mud
verbs.why: A storm can knock out the power in a whole town, and one broken cable knocked out the internet at the airport. The flood knocked out the park's only water pipeline.

verbs.wrong: To stop the supply of something
verbs.why: The doctor told him to cut down on salt, and many families cut down on driving when gas prices rise. Visitors to the park were asked to cut down on showers.

verbs.wrong: To fail to happen as planned
verbs.why: A student who misses two weeks of class falls behind, and a building project falls behind when the rain does not stop. The $208 million pipeline upgrade may now fall behind schedule.

verbs.correct: To block an area so no one enters
verbs.wrong: To end a business for good
verbs.why: Police close off a street after an accident, and a museum closes off a room during repairs. On September 3 the park closed off more trails, with no reopening date.

mainIdea.s: A flash flood hit the bottom of the Grand Canyon, and about 80 people were rescued by helicopter. Two people died, one is missing, and the park's only water pipeline is badly damaged.
mainIdea.why: Rescue teams saved about 80 people over the weekend of August 29 and 30, two hikers from Texas died, a third friend is missing, and about 40 percent of the pipeline is damaged.

mainIdea.s: A sudden flood at the bottom of the Grand Canyon killed two hikers and left a third one missing. Rescue teams saved about 80 people, and the water pipeline escaped without damage.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the flood damaged about 40 percent of the park's only water pipeline, and the South Rim has about two weeks of water in storage.

mainIdea.s: A wildfire on the North Rim of the Grand Canyon forced hundreds of visitors to leave the park. The fire destroyed a historic lodge and closed the main trails for the rest of the summer.
mainIdea.why: The event was a flash flood, not a fire. The Dragon Bravo Fire happened in July 2025, and its burn scar only matters because bare ground makes rain flow faster.

lines.text: Did you hear about the flash flood at the Grand Canyon last weekend?
Just the headline. Something about helicopters?
Right. A flood {{swept through}} Bright Angel Canyon on Saturday afternoon, right by Phantom Ranch. Rescue teams {{brought in}} helicopters and searched with night vision after dark.
How many people were down there?
About 80. Forty-five were rescued by Saturday night, and the rest were {{flown out}} on Sunday.
[[Thank goodness for that]]. Was anyone hurt?
Two men from Texas died, and a third friend, a pilot from Wyoming, is still missing. Searchers {{kept on}} looking all week with dogs and drones.
[[My heart goes out to]] their families. They had just {{set out}} on a fishing trip, right?
Yes, several days of hiking and fishing. They last {{checked in with}} their families that Thursday.
How did the rangers even know who was missing?
They {{went through}} the permit records and checked license plates.
Smart. And what about the park itself?
The flood {{knocked out}} the only water pipeline. About 40 percent of it is damaged, and the South Rim has around two weeks of water in storage.
[[That's the last thing they need]]. So what are they doing?
Hotels stopped taking overnight guests, and visitors have to {{cut down on}} showers. And the big pipeline upgrade will probably {{fall behind}} schedule now.
[[Talk about bad timing]]. Is the canyon open at all?
The rims are open, but on Wednesday they {{closed off}} more of the inner trails. No reopening date yet.
Still, with 80 people rescued and nobody hurt in the evacuation, [[it could have been a lot worse]].

expressions.def: Used to show relief when you hear that something bad did not happen
ex: Everyone got home before the snow started. Thank goodness for that.
The test result was negative. Thank goodness for that.

expressions.def: Used to say that you feel deep sympathy for people who are suffering
ex: My heart goes out to everyone who lost their home in the fire.
My heart goes out to the driver's family.

expressions.expr: That's the last thing they need
expressions.def: Used to say that a new problem is especially bad for people who already have problems
ex: Another storm this week? That's the last thing the farmers need.
The bus is late, too. That's the last thing they need right now.

expressions.def: Used to say that something happened at the worst possible moment
ex: The rain started just as the wedding began. Talk about bad timing.
He lost his job the week they bought the house. Talk about bad timing.

expressions.expr: It could have been a lot worse
expressions.def: Used to say that a bad situation was not as bad as it might have been
ex: We lost the trailer, but nobody was hurt. It could have been a lot worse.
Only one flight was canceled. It could have been a lot worse.
